newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief urges direct talks by Cypriot leaders.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief urges direct talks by Cypriot leaders.

text.p: Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali warned on Wednesday of a false sense of stability on the divided island of Cyprus and called for direct talks between the leaders of the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities to negotiate an overall agreement.

In a written report to the Security Council, he also urged both sides to move away from "polemics and mutual accusations" and to implement a series of goodwill measures, including bicommunal contacts and joint projects.

Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since 1974 when Turkish troops landed in the north in reaction to a coup in Nicosia by the military government then ruling Greece. The United Nations has since been trying to reunite the island on the agreed basis of a bicommunal, bizonal federation.
"The apparent calm that has prevailed for some years has lulled political leaders and the people of both communities into a false sense of stability," Boutros-Ghali said.

"Beneath the surface, however, the situation in Cyprus is changing, in terms both of the demographic composition of the island and of the relationship of the two communities with each other and to the outside world."

The two communities would either take control of their destiny by reaching an overall settlement on the basis already agreed, "or forces beyond their control will fundamentally change the situation on the island," he said.

"An urgent effort is accordingly required in 1997 to bring about early direct talks between the two leaders...to negotiate an overall agreement. Both leaders should clearly and publicly commit themselves to such a process," he added, refering to Greek Cypriot leader Glafcos Clerides, president of the internationally-recognised government of Cyprus, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash, president of a Turkish Cypriot state proclaimed in 1983 which only Ankara recognises.

The secretary-general said more intensive contacts with the two leaders, and with Greece and Turkey, were planned for the new year, and he called on those two countries to become more active in support of the U.N. good offices mission.

Stressing the need to create an atmosphere of confidence and reconcilation, he said both leaders "must give tangible indications that they are seeking an overall settlement on the basis of one country and to ensure that their words and deeds are in harmony with that objective."
